title: When a Robot Fails, What Does the Data Say?
summary: Learn how robotics teams can preserve sensor data, software versions, and access histories to answer customer questions.
body_markdown:
*After an incident occurs, customers typically ask four questions. A training pipeline can usually offer rough answers to those questions, but it can rarely provide proof.*


The message comes in on a Tuesday: one of your robots did something it shouldn’t have at a customer site. Nobody was hurt, but the customer’s operations lead wants a full account of what happened by Friday. Your team pulls the footage from the training dataset, lines it up with the logs, and within a few hours can explain roughly what went wrong. What it can’t do is actually *prove* any of it.


That gap catches many physical AI teams off guard, because they already keep plenty of field data. They keep it to feed the data flywheel, the loop that turns a fleet’s failures into training data to improve the next model. But robotics data retention has to support incident investigations, too. The data that teaches a robot and the data that proves what it did are the same recordings, but they’re held to different standards, and most teams only build for the first of these jobs. The customer’s questions tend to arrive in the same order, and each one exposes a different gap.

## Robotics data retention starts with what the robot saw


“What did the robot see?” is often the first question. The customer wants the full record of the moment, but a training clip is an edited version of it. Curation is designed to only keep what matters to the model: the frames around the failure, re-encoded to save space, sometimes downsampled, and often stripped of the sensor streams the model doesn’t use. Each of those choices makes sense for training, and each one removes important context the customer is now asking for.


Expect questions about what happened in the seconds before the failure, what the other sensors registered, and what the operator did after taking over. Answering those questions requires the raw, synchronized streams from every sensor for a window around the event. So the raw data has to survive long enough for someone to ask. Our post on[keeping fleet data](https://www.backblaze.com/blog/the-physical-ai-data-flywheel-only-works-if-you-keep-the-data/) covers what usually stops it from surviving. When an incident occurs, the point is narrower: the clip in the training set is a summary, and the customer is asking for the source.


## What was it running?


Every incident record has to show exactly which model and software build the robot was running when it happened. That’s harder than it sounds, because over-the-air updates mean a fleet rarely runs a single version. Some robots pick up a release on day one, others a week later, and a few get held back for testing. Without a record that ties the event to a specific build, nobody on the team can say whether this is a bug that was fixed last month or a new one.


That matters because the customer’s underlying question is whether it could happen again, and the answer to that question starts with what the robot was running. A team that can name the build, and trace the model in it back to the data that trained it, can give a direct answer. A team that can’t is left offering reassurances it has no way to back up.


## How do we know nothing was changed?


Training workflows are built to change data, and evidence is data nobody has changed. Relabeling, cropping, transcoding, and overwriting are normal work in a training pipeline, and each one is reasonable on its own. Each one also makes the record harder to stand behind. If the only copy of an incident recording was re-encoded last month for a new labeling pass, the team has to explain why it can’t produce the original, and even an innocent edit raises a question nobody can fully answer.


The fix is to separate the two jobs. The original recording of an incident gets locked against changes and deletion for a set period, and the training pipeline keeps working from it by reference. Datasets point to the locked file, and anything the team derives is written as a new object beside it. The team can relabel and crop as much as it likes, and the record of what happened stays exactly as the robot captured it.


## Who else has touched it?


Most teams can’t produce an access history for a single recording. Training buckets are shared by design. Perception engineers, labelers, evaluation scripts, and a handful of service accounts all read from them, and some of them write. When the customer asks who has had access to the footage since the incident, “probably just the perception team” isn’t an answer that builds confidence.


A log of every read and write, kept alongside the data, makes that an easy question to answer. And customers won’t be the only ones asking it. Insurers and regulators are still working out how to evaluate robots operating in the real world, and their questions look a lot like the customer’s.


## Where Backblaze fits


Accountability is decided before incidents even occur. The record a team can produce on its worst day is whatever its storage already preserved: the original sensor recordings, the model and software versions tied to the event, and the history of access to that data. Backblaze B2 Cloud Storage provides the storage foundation for preserving those records.


Object Lock in compliance mode keeps a recording from being altered or deleted until its retention date passes, even by an administrator. For a specific incident, a legal hold can freeze the recording for as long as the conversation with the customer runs. Both are set through the S3-compatible API, so the tools a team already uses to write data can apply them. Bucket access logs show who read or wrote each object, which answers the last question with a record instead of a guess. Backblaze’s SOC 2 Type 2 attestation supports deployments in regulated industries, and every object is stored in an always-hot tier, so the full recording is ready the day the customer, insurer, or regulator asks, with plenty of time to spare.
